locator: ASHP report 'Severity and Impact of Sterile Fluid Shortages' (as of Oct. 25, 2024): PDF p.1 introduction and Key Findings; PDF p.3 'Changes to Inventory Levels' table (days on hand of large-volume fluids)
shows: ASHP surveyed its members 16-25 October 2024 (401 participants answering at least part of the questionnaire). Of 191 respondents responsible for purchasing or inventory who answered, baseline days on hand of large-volume fluids were 1 week or less for 8%, 1 to 2 weeks for 21%, 2 weeks to 1 month for 32%, 1 to 3 months for 35%, 3 to 6 months for 4% and 6 months or more for 1%. At the time of the survey the same bands were 16%, 30%, 30%, 23%, 1% and 0%, and ASHP reports that 47% were down to two weeks' supply or less. Among the 139 at facilities where Baxter was the primary supplier, baseline was 8%, 19%, 32%, 36%, 4% and 1% and current 19%, 32%, 29%, 19%, 0% and 0%.
limits: Self-reported banded days on hand from pharmacy staff at facilities that answered, not measured stock, and more than one respondent may describe the same facility. The bands are wide, so no mean or median can be read off. Baseline was reported during the shortage and may be recalled with error. Large-volume fluids (250 mL or more) are not the same as resuscitation fluids. Baseline inventory was widely spread, with about 40% of respondents holding more than a month, so no single typical figure represents it.

locator: PMC author manuscript PMC8096207 of Crit Care Med 2019;47(11):1582-1590: Abstract (Design, Setting, Patients, Measurements and Main Results); Discussion, limitations paragraph
shows: Retrospective cohort of 1,032 adults with severe sepsis or septic shock treated in the emergency department of one urban tertiary centre, January 2014 to May 2017. 509 (49.3%) received a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus within three hours of sepsis onset. Overall mortality was 17.1%, and 20.4% in the shock group. Missing the three-hour target was associated with higher odds of in-hospital mortality (OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.03-2.24), delayed hypotension (OR 1.42) and about 2 days longer ICU stay, controlling for sex, end-stage renal disease, heart failure, severity, obesity, a sepsis mortality score and time to antibiotics. Higher fluid volumes by three hours correlated with lower mortality, plateauing between 35 and 45 mL/kg.

shows: A preliminary, non-peer-reviewed analysis of Truveta electronic health records covered people aged 12 and older with emergency-department encounters for nausea or vomiting (277,500 encounters) or dehydration (68,246) between 1 January and 13 October 2024. The absolute falls are 3.5 and 4.1 percentage points, relative falls of about 64% and 62%, so the labelled figures should not be used. The data were preliminary as of 23 October 2024, cover Truveta member health systems only, and the authors say saline use may be under-captured.

locator: PubMed abstract, PMID 28322415 (JAMA 2017;317(14):1433-1442): Design, Setting, and Participants; Exposures; Results
shows: Retrospective cohort of 27,835 adults with septic shock admitted July 2008 to June 2013 to 26 U.S. hospitals in the Premier Healthcare Database that used norepinephrine for at least 60% of such patients at baseline. A shortage quarter was any 2011 quarter in which a hospital's norepinephrine use fell by more than 20% from baseline. Norepinephrine use fell from 77.0% of patients to a low of 55.7%, with phenylephrine the most common alternative. Admission in a shortage quarter was associated with higher in-hospital mortality: 777 of 1,961 patients (39.6%) against 9,283 of 25,874 (35.9%) in normal quarters, an absolute risk increase of 3.7% (95% CI 1.5%-6.0%) and an adjusted odds ratio of 1.15 (95% CI 1.01-1.30).
limits: This was a vasopressor shortage, not an IV-fluid shortage. Patients in shortage quarters were treated with substitutes, so the estimate reflects substitution, not withheld therapy. The cohort had very high baseline mortality, and the result is an observational association at the hospital-quarter level that may be confounded. Hospitals were selected for high baseline norepinephrine use. Only the abstract was read, so the adjustment set, sensitivity analyses and the authors' limitations were not checked.

locator: Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Limited letter to NSE and BSE dated 26 March 2023, 'Sub: Update on IT Security Incident', paragraphs 1-4. Single-page PDF (printed and PDF page 1).
shows: In a 26 March 2023 letter to India's stock exchanges, Sun Pharma updated its 2 March 2023 disclosure of an IT security incident. A ransomware group had claimed responsibility. The company believed the incident's effect on its IT systems included a breach of certain file systems and the theft of company data and personal data. As part of containment it proactively isolated its network and began recovery. It said that as a result of these measures its business operations had been impacted, so revenues were expected to be reduced in some of its businesses. It would incur expenses for the incident and remediation and could not yet determine other potential adverse impacts. The letter attributes the operational impact to these containment measures.
limits: This is the company's own forward-looking statement in a listing disclosure, made 24 days after its first intimation. It quantifies nothing: no revenue amount, duration, business line, product or market is named. It does not say whether manufacturing, quality release, order processing or shipping stopped, so it cannot calibrate a halt duration or a lost-output or permanent-loss fraction. It says nothing about shortages, customers or patients; the absence of a shortage statement is not evidence that no shortage occurred. The letter does not name the ransomware group; attribution to ALPHV/BlackCat comes from secondary reporting. The realized revenue effect is not reported here. Sun Pharma is a diversified generic and specialty drug maker, not a concentrated sterile IV-fluid producer, so any transfer to SC10's supplier needs an explicit argument.

locator: UnitedHealth Group press release 'UnitedHealth Group Updates on Change Healthcare Cyberattack', dated April 22, 2024: headline and date; section 'Change Healthcare Service Restoration', paragraphs 1-5. HTML page without page numbers.
shows: On 22 April 2024 UnitedHealth said Change Healthcare had prioritized restoring services that affect patient access to care or medication. Pharmacy services were back to near-normal levels, with 99% of pre-incident pharmacies able to process claims. Medical claims were flowing at near-normal levels as systems came back online or providers switched to other ways of submitting them, though a small number of providers remained adversely affected. Payment processing, which it said represents about 6% of all payments in the US health care system, was at about 86% of pre-incident levels. About 80% of Change functionality on the major platforms and products had been restored, and full restoration of other systems was expected in the coming weeks.
limits: Self-reported status figures with undefined bases ('pre-incident pharmacies', 'functionality'); nobody outside the company checked them. The pharmacy figure counts pharmacies able to process claims, not transaction volume or patient access. Near-normal medical-claim flows include providers who moved to other submission routes, so they are not the clearinghouse's own recovery alone. The page is the company's live newsroom copy retrieved in 2026. The elapsed time since identification (61 days, using the 21 February 2024 date in the company's 8-K) is arithmetic across documents. Full IT restoration of a transaction clearinghouse took longer than two months, which shows how long the tail of IT recovery can be, but it is not a production or distribution recovery and does not establish a manufacturing halt duration.

locator: Form 8-K (date of report February 21, 2024; signed February 22, 2024), Item 1.05 'Material Cybersecurity Incidents', paragraphs 1-4. EDGAR HTML, single page.
shows: UnitedHealth Group's Item 1.05 filing states that on 21 February 2024 it identified that a suspected nation-state associated threat actor had gained access to some Change Healthcare IT systems. On detection it proactively isolated the impacted systems from other connecting systems. It could not estimate the duration or extent of the disruption, and warned that certain networks and transactional services might not be accessible during it. It believed the network interruption was specific to Change Healthcare systems, with all other company systems operational, and had not determined that the incident was reasonably likely to materially affect its financial condition or results.
limits: An initial filing made the day after detection. Its attribution to a suspected nation-state actor was not sustained: the company's quarterly report for Q1 2024 describes cybercrime threat actors. It does not mention ransomware, name the attacker or list the affected services, and gives no restoration estimate. The materiality statement is an early disclosure judgment that the company's later cost reporting overtook. The filing describes inaccessible networks and transactional services, not interrupted manufacture or distribution of a physical product, so it is at most a weak analog for a supply shortage. Disruption from the victim's own isolation of systems is not separated from damage done by the attacker.

valid_for.incident: Change Healthcare cyberattack identified 21 February 2024
valid_for.system: Change Healthcare information technology systems (UnitedHealth Group)

related.note: The Q1 2024 10-Q revises the attribution to cybercrime threat actors and reports the costs this filing could not estimate.

locator: Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 31, 2024 (dated May 8, 2024), Part I, Item 2 (MD&A): 'Change Healthcare Cyberattack', paragraphs 1-2 (printed p. 14); 'Business Trends', 'Medical Cost Trends', paragraph 2 (printed p. 15). EDGAR HTML.
shows: UnitedHealth's Q1 2024 10-Q says that on 21 February 2024 it identified that cybercrime threat actors had gained access to certain Change Healthcare IT systems. For the three months to 31 March 2024 it incurred $593 million of direct response costs, including network restoration and increased medical care expenditures. Optum Insight had estimated business disruption impacts of $279 million, reflecting lost revenue while maintaining full readiness of the affected Change Healthcare services. To support care providers it accelerated funding and provided interest-free loans of about $3.9 billion through 31 March 2024, over $6.5 billion through 30 April 2024. It separately reports $340 million of Q1 medical costs from temporarily suspending some care management activities, and says the disruption affected claims receipt timing for payer customers. It expected further response costs and disruption impacts through the rest of the year.
limits: Company-reported, unaudited quarterly figures in nominal 2024 US dollars. The $279 million is an estimate that combines lost revenue with the cost of keeping the affected services ready; the filing does not split the two or say how much revenue was deferred rather than lost. It does not say whether the $340 million is part of the $593 million. Loans and accelerated funding are advances to providers, not losses, and do not measure providers' own disruption costs, though their size indicates how widely cash flow was disrupted downstream. The figures cover one quarter and were expected to grow. The victim is a claims and payment clearinghouse inside a diversified insurer, not a manufacturer; none of the costs relate to physical product output or shortage, and they cannot be transferred to an IV-fluid maker's daily output value or permanent-loss fraction.
